2451.dq: Every lexical word requires at least one major syllable (there are some function words that do not) ... There are four lexical tones.
2451.prule: No word-stress rule stated. Uipo/Khoibu is described as a lexical tone language: four lexical tones (Chao 53, 22, 41, 44) borne by 'major' syllables; 'minor' syllables (open, short schwa) carry no contrastive tone and get a short falling contour in isolation; every lexical word has at least one major syllable, commonly in sesquisyllabic minor+major shape. Stress, accent and prominence are never mentioned.
2451.quote: Uipo has a difference between major and minor syllables (following the terminology of Butler (2015)). Every lexical word requires at least one major syllable (there are some function words that do not), and major syllables can be closed or open, and they can have one of the four possible consonant clusters in onset position. Closed syllables can have either a long or a short vowel, but open syllables have to have either a long vowel or a diphthong. Minor syllables, on the other hand, are always open, and always have a short schwa as their vowel. Minor syllables do not seem to have contrastive…

A full-text search of the article for stress/accent/prominence/weight/rhythm gives zero hits. Earlier descriptions (L.B. Singh 2013 §1.7 'Khoibu is a tonal language and there are three tones... rising, level and falling'; L.B. Singh 2015 'Khoibu Tone'; S.I. Singh 2016) analyse three tones; S.I. Singh 2016 abstract: 'the study of suprasegmental includes only tone. Khoibu does not have juncture.' Singh 2015's remark that high-toned vowels 'are articulated with a greater force of breath and are heard as tense' concerns tone realisation, not stress.

2454.prule: Word stress is lexically determined and lexically contrastive (Table 2.10: káɫi/kɑɫí, táɾu/tɑɾú, béɫu/beɫú, tóri/torí, gáɫi/gaɫí); in underived words it falls on the final or the penultimate syllable (disyllables: final or initial; trisyllables: penult or final), with no phonological rule predicting which. Not weight-sensitive: vowel length is not phonemic and phonetic length is a consequence of stress (sec. 2.2.1.3).
2454.srule: No rhythmic secondary stress is described. Secondary stress occurs only as a demoted lexical stress in complex forms: in compounds the first element's primary stress becomes secondary (baša̍r.dóyu); when a stress-bearing suffix takes the primary stress the stem's stressed syllable carries the secondary mark (noʋés → noʋe̍s-gíni); an originally stressed prefix keeps secondary stress before a vowel-initial word (be̍.izzatí, na̍.umét).
2454.quote: In Khowar, word stress is lexically determined; that is, in each word a specific syllable is stressed. Stress has several functions in Khowar. 2454.tone: Sec. 2.2.1.2 'Tone' (pp. 34-35): 'In Khowar, a low-rising pitch, accompanied by extended duration (length) contrasts with high-falling pitch in a small number of pairs' (don ‘tooth’ vs doón ‘ghee’, bas vs baás ‘flame’, sarék vs sareék); 'Given the limited number of minimal pairs in which tone is contrastive, it seems appropriate to say that tone plays a relatively minor role in Khowar, and it can be considered only partially a tone language.' Bashir analyses the low tone as stress on the second mora of a lengthened vowel (fn. 28); Liljegren & Khan 2017 (p. 225): 'a number of items have a low tone, lexically assigned to a vowel... stress is associated with the locus of the low tone'. Strand 2012 recasts the same contrast as anterior vs posterior 'accented phonation'. Stress is the primary word-prosodic system; the tone contrast is marginal and rides on the stressed syllable, so tone or pitch accent would overstate it.

2455.prule: Word accent is 'fundamentally the same as in New Persian': the default position is the last syllable of the word (Eilers speaks of the 'Endbetonung der Einzelwörter' and 'der Endakzent des Wortes', and the glossary marks accent only where it is NOT on the last syllable); inflectional suffixes take the stress (plural -ā́ 'betontem -ā', deictic/determinative -ä́ 'stets betontes -ä'). No reference to syllable weight or syllable count: quantity-insensitive final stress. Translation of the quote: 'The accent is fundamentally the same as in New Persian. Other dialects too, and not least New Persian, fluctuate in their stressing, in that within a sentence-whole the final stress of the individual words often appears suspended (sandhi effect). The accent does not always appear in the sentence at the place where one expects it; so too in NP yekí for yéki, digarí for digári etc. In Chunsari the initial stressing of the word that begins the sentence stands out strongly, i.e. the first syllable of the sentence (except vä, o "and") very often receives a strong accent which drowns out the word's final accent... At the end of the sentence lies the other major stress position... The plural is formed by adding stressed -ā... The accent is marked only where it does not lie on the last syllable.'

2456.tone: Lexical tone on every full syllable. Owen 2012:12 (first-hand, publisher text, opened): 'while some contemporary speakers have a tone system with six tones, most speakers have only five tones.' Egerød 1959:124 (publisher scan, opened): 'There are six tones.' Owen 2012:17 on Gedney's 1964 field notes, published 1994: 'Gedney identified six distinctive tones' (second-hand; Gedney/Hudak 1994 not opened). On stress, the only statement in any opened source is Owen 2017:141 relaying Petsuk 1978:26-29: stressed syllables in polysyllabic morphemes have the full C(C)V(C)T template; unstressed syllables are CVT with vowel normally [a] and a highly restricted but not absent tone. Owen 2017:146-147 also speaks of 'phonological minor syllables' (examples 13-14) beside 'the main phonological syllable', but gives no placement statement. No source says which position is stressed; the reduced-[a]-presyllable pattern suggests the familiar Southwestern-Tai non-final minor syllable (hence final prominence), but that is an inference not stated in any page opened.

2458.prule: Main stress on the penultimate syllable of the word, quantity-insensitive and counted from the right edge; recomputed over the whole word when suffixes are added (ako'me, akoma'ge, akomagĩ're). 2458.tone: Kikuyu is a two-tone (H, L) plus downstep language (Englebretson & Wa-Ngatho 2015 sec. 1.4, p. 9; Clements 1984), and the modern open descriptions in the copy consulted (Englebretson & Wa-Ngatho 2015, Clements 1984, Githinji 2014, Muthui 2001, Bennett et al. 1985) describe tone only and state no stress rule. Barlow's own 'TONE' section (p. 7) covers only emphatic vowel lengthening / pitch raising and falling interrogative intonation. Armstrong 1940, The Phonetic and Tonal Structure of Kikuyu, ch. XXIII 'Stress', sec. 516 (Google Books, the 2017 reprint, id 4r02DwAAQBAJ, RA1-PA38; grade excerpt): 'Stress in unemphatic speech has little importance in Kikuyu, whereas tone and length are immensely important. A weak stress occurs generally on the penultimate syllable, and is independent of tone. This stress is often so weak that, without reinforcement, it is impossible to distinguish it as being stronger than that on adjacent syllables.' So the stress is weak, non-contrastive and orthogonal to the tone system; every source that mentions it (Hinde 1904, McGregor 1905, Barlow 1914, Armstrong 1940) places it on the penult.

tn.quote: Dado que el acento en kiliwa es un complejo de tono y de intensidad, se le debe denominar acento tónico. ... 2471.dflt: Initial syllable full (main) stress, light medial syllables unstressed, final syllable secondary stress, e.g. /kudike/ 'cooking pot' (p. 33); the initial rule applies to every word whatever its weight profile.
2471.prule: Non-contrastive stress; every word-initial syllable has full stress, and a simple lexeme shows one main stress, on the first syllable (the root vowel), irrespective of that syllable's weight.
2471.srule: Every word-final syllable has secondary stress; a word-medial syllable has full (non-main) stress if it is heavy (long vowel, or short vowel closed by the first half of a geminate) and no stress if light; main stress stays on the initial syllable (light-medial default: initial main + final secondary, e.g. /kudike/; heavy medial adds a stress, e.g. /nu:putti/).

2472.dq: The prominence of stress in Kodi is culminative in that only one syllable will ever occupy the maximally prominent peak within a stress domain. This means that every word only has one stressed syllable, regardless of whether it is a disyllabic word or trisyllabic word.
2472.dloc: Sec. 2.3 'Stress', p. 316 (proofs p. 5); sec. 4.1 'Stress and syllable reduplication', pp. 335-339, examples (58)-(65) and Tables 7-10; also p. 322, sec. 3.3.3 ('stress which is mostly penultimate and antepenultimate in Kodi').
2472.prule: One culminative primary stress per word, never on the final syllable. Disyllabic stems: penultimate ('normally', p. 335: otu, ɓuri, ihha, mete). Trisyllabic stems: antepenultimate or penultimate, lexically determined per item; in the source's own list (60) four of five bases are antepenultimate (ˈuɗoko 'kiss', ˈmbihoko 'deflated', ˈɓokolo 'big', ˈɗoŋgolo 'catch'; macrons in the typeset proofs) and one is penultimate (taˈŋaro 'look up'; also stem-penult in pa-teˈrohi), with duration/intensity/pitch measurements for both patterns (Tables 7-10). Stress is computed on the stem: the productive causative prefix pa- is outside the stress domain (pa-ˈrahi, pa-ˈhaɣi, pa-ˈɓokolo, pa-teˈrohi; ma-ˈtodi). Net: right-edge two-syllable window (penult/antepenult) over the stem with lexical choice in trisyllables; no weight conditioning stated.
2472.srule: None: 'every word only has one stressed syllable, regardless of whether it is a disyllabic word or trisyllabic word' (stress culminative; at most one foot per base; a single stress marked per word, incl. four-syllable ka.ˈtu.ɗi.lo). No secondary or rhythmic stress described.
